What should I include when asking for a process recommendation?

A shaft or sleeve will usually start with turning. A housing with pockets and flat mounting faces is more likely to need milling. Angled features or access to several faces may call for a multi-axis setup. Some parts need a combination; send the drawing so we can review the sequence.

Compare the processes by geometry
Route to discuss	Geometry cues	Drawing and quote questions
CNC turning	Rotational features such as a shaft, sleeve, disc or fitting, often arranged around an axis.	Define the datum axis, diameters, shoulders, grooves, threads and runout if required. Confirm whether cross-holes, flats or slots need secondary milling.
CNC milling	Block-like or irregular forms with pockets, slots, holes, contours and planar mounting faces.	Define datum faces, pocket depth, hole patterns and positional relationships. Confirm stock, clamping surfaces, setups and inspection records.
Multi-axis machining	Features distributed over several faces, angled faces or areas that need different tool approaches.	Define common datums, face-to-face and angular relationships. Review tool access, workholding and sequence against the model.
When does a part need more than one process?

A shaft with cross-holes, a turned fitting with milled flats or a housing with angled faces may need more than one operation or setup. The route should preserve the relationships between critical features. Send a 3D model and controlled 2D drawing so the team can review datums, access and inspection together.

Is 5-axis machining always more accurate?

No single process label guarantees accuracy. Acceptance depends on the part geometry, machine and setup, datum strategy, material, finishing and measurement method. If an interface matters, state its tolerance and datum on the drawing and ask how it will be produced and checked. Any tolerance target needs feature-specific review.

What should I include when asking for a process recommendation?
A 3D model and the controlling 2D drawing revision.
Material grade and condition, or the functional requirement if still undecided.
Quantity for the first order and expected repeat pattern, if known.
Critical datums, fits, surface requirements and required inspection records.
Finish, packaging and required arrival date, with any standards or approvals identified.

Use the RFQ checklist to organize those details. We review your drawing before confirming the machining process and quoting a price and schedule.
